title: Psalm 71: Do Not Forsake Me When I Am Old
summary: An aging believer who has trusted God since birth prays not to be cast off in old age, when enemies whisper that God has abandoned him. He asks for rescue, promises to keep praising God more and more, and longs to live long enough to tell the next generation of God's power. The psalm ends with harp and lyre, celebrating the God who has redeemed him.
story: Psalm 71 is the prayer of a lifetime. Coming just before the royal psalm that closes Book II, it looks back over many years of God's faithfulness and forward to the end of life. In a book full of young men in danger, here is an old man who has seen many troubles and still expects God to bring him back up from the depths. Many scholars read Psalms 70 and 71 as closely linked: Psalm 71 has no heading, it shares several phrases with Psalm 70 (the plea to hurry, the shaming of those who seek his harm), and some Hebrew manuscripts join the two. Whether originally one poem or two placed side by side, they read well together, the short cry of Psalm 70 opening into the long reflection of Psalm 71.
historical:
Psalm 71 has no superscription in the Hebrew text, which is unusual in Book II, where nearly every psalm has one. The Greek translation known as the Septuagint (the Jewish translation of the Hebrew Scriptures into Greek, made in the last centuries before Christ) adds a heading attributing it to David, and many traditional readers take it as a prayer of the aged David, perhaps from the time of Absalom's revolt or the troubles at the end of his reign (1 Kings 1). Other scholars see the speaker as an unnamed older worshiper, possibly a temple singer, since he promises to praise God with harp and lyre. The psalm itself doesn't say, and no event is named.

What is clear is that the psalm draws heavily on earlier prayers. Verses 1 to 3 closely follow Psalm 31:1-3; verses 5 and 6 echo Psalm 22:9-10 on trusting God from the womb; verse 12 recalls the cry of Psalm 22:11 and Psalm 38:21-22; and verse 13 borrows from Psalm 35. The speaker prays in the words of the psalms he has known all his life, which fits the portrait of a person who was taught by God from his youth.
cultural:
Old age in ancient Israel carried both honor and danger. The law commanded respect for the elderly (Leviticus 19:32), and gray hair could be a crown of glory (Proverbs 16:31). But the old were also vulnerable. When strength failed, they depended on family and community for protection, and enemies could exploit that weakness. The taunt in verse 11, “God has forsaken him”, reflects a common assumption: if an old man is sick, poor, or unprotected, God must have abandoned him.

Verse 7 says the speaker has become “a portent to many”, a sign or wonder. Some take this to mean that his troubles made people see him as an example of divine judgment; others read it more positively, as a man whose preservation through so many troubles has become a sign of God's care. The harp (nebel) and lyre (kinnor) in verse 22 were the stringed instruments of Israel's temple worship, played by the Levitical singers. The expectation in verse 18 that the old should teach the next generation reflects Israel's pattern of passing on the story of God's deeds within families (Deuteronomy 6:6-7; Psalm 78:4).
literary: The psalm moves back and forth between petition and praise rather than following a straight line from lament to thanksgiving. Verses 1 to 4 ask for refuge; verses 5 to 8 look back to birth and youth; verses 9 to 13 turn to old age and the enemies' threats; verses 14 to 16 pledge continued hope and praise; verses 17 and 18 return to youth and old age together; and verses 19 to 24 rise into confident praise. The words always, all day long, and more and more recur, giving a sense of unbroken, lifelong devotion. Righteousness (tsedaqah) appears five times, often as the content of the speaker's praise. The psalm ends with the enemies disgraced, answering the petition of verse 13 and completing the arc from plea to fulfilled hope.

outline.t: Do not forsake me in old age
I will hope and praise more and more
Taught from youth, telling the next generation
God will revive me once again

doctrines.note: The speaker traces God's care from the womb through youth into old age. God's providence isn't limited to dramatic rescues; it covers the whole span of a life, including its slow decline.

Hope in this psalm is rooted in memory. Because God has been faithful from birth, the speaker expects him to be faithful in old age, and even to bring him back up “from the depths of the earth” (verse 20).
Verse 18 asks for time to proclaim God's power to the next generation. Faith in Israel was handed down, and the old carried a particular calling to pass on what they had seen God do.

words.note: Ziqnah, old age. It appears in verse 9, and verse 18 adds the related picture of gray hair. The psalm is one of the few prayers in Scripture written from the vantage point of old age, when strength fails and the fear of being discarded is real.

Tsedaqah, righteousness. It appears five times in the psalm. God's righteousness is his faithfulness to do what is right, especially to rescue those who trust him. The speaker appeals to it for rescue (verse 2) and makes it the theme of his lifelong testimony (verses 15, 16, 19, 24).
Tiqvah, hope. In verse 5 God himself is the speaker's hope. It comes from a verb meaning to wait for or look eagerly toward, and in the Psalms it describes confident expectation that God will act.

Mopheth, a wonder, sign, or portent. It is often used of the signs God performed in Egypt. In verse 7 the speaker himself has become a sign to many, whether as a warning or as evidence of God's care, and scholars read the phrase both ways.

christ: The New Testament doesn't quote Psalm 71, and its link to Jesus is thematic. The enemies' taunt that God has forsaken the speaker and no one will rescue him anticipates the mockery at the cross, when bystanders said God should deliver Jesus if he wanted him (Matthew 27:43). Jesus himself cried out as one forsaken (Mark 15:34), and the hope of verse 20, that God would bring the sufferer back up from the depths of the earth, found its fullest answer in his resurrection. Christians also read the psalm's confidence about aging in light of the resurrection: the one who has trusted God from the womb can face weakness and death, because the God who raised Jesus will not discard those who belong to him.
questions: The speaker has trusted God since his youth. What memories of God's faithfulness in your past help you trust him now?
Verse 18 asks God for time to tell the next generation about him. Who has passed faith on to you, and to whom might you pass it on?
How does the fear of weakness or aging affect you, and what in this psalm speaks to that fear?
